title: Faster 64-bit signed floor division by constants
excerpt: A new algorithm speeds up full-range signed 64-bit floor division by up to 20% on ARM and 10% on x86.
body:
A service that needs to compute whole days from a Unix timestamp often writes `timestamp / 86400`. In most languages that expression uses the hardware division instruction, which on a 64-bit core can take dozens of cycles.

When the divisor is a constant, a multiplication by a pre-computed magic number and a shift can replace the division and run in a handful of cycles. The author of the “fast-floordiv” page measured a throughput improvement of 10, 20 % on ARM and 5, 10 % on x86 for the divisor 86400, compared with the built-in operator.

The post explains why floor division, division that rounds toward −∞, is useful, shows the limits of existing fast algorithms, and then introduces a new approach that beats them on most 64-bit divisors. The reader will see benchmark numbers, a ready-to-copy implementation for the common divisor 86400, and a short guide on how to integrate it.

## Why floor division matters and is missing in many languages

Signed integer floor division returns the mathematical floor of the exact quotient, unlike the usual truncated division that rounds toward 0. For positive divisors the two results differ only when the dividend is negative; for negative divisors the difference appears for any non-multiple. Calculations such as date arithmetic, interval bucketing, and Euclidean algorithms need the floor behavior because it guarantees a non-negative remainder.

Despite this need, mainstream compilers and languages such as C, C++, Go, and Swift do not expose a floor-division operator. They only provide the truncated `/` operator. Some libraries implement floor division, but the implementations are often the naïve `a / b` followed by an adjustment, which is slower than a dedicated algorithm. The source notes that at least one prominent library shipped a buggy overflow-prone version for four years, underscoring how little attention the operation receives.

## Existing fast algorithms and their limitations

The classic fast-division technique described in *Hacker’s Delight* replaces division by a constant `d` with a multiplication by a “magic” multiplier `M` and a right shift. The multiplier is derived from `⌊2ⁿ / d⌋` for a suitable `n`. This works well for unsigned division and for signed truncating division, but floor division adds two complications:

1. The sign of the divisor changes the rounding direction, so a separate correction step is needed.  
2. The multiplier must be chosen to avoid overflow for the full 64-bit signed range. Many published generators produce values that overflow when the dividend is `INT64_MIN`.

Because of these issues, existing fast floor-division code often falls back to the hardware division for edge cases, or adds extra branches that hurt throughput. The author observed that typical online searches and LLM prompts surface only these slower variants, leaving a performance gap for the common case of a known constant divisor.

## The new approach and its benchmark results

The new method builds on the magic-multiplier idea but selects `M` from a 128-bit intermediate (`__int128`) to guarantee correctness across the entire signed range. For the divisor 86400 the multiplier is:

```cpp
const int64_t M = ((__int128(1) << 79) / 86400 + 1);
```

Using this multiplier, the division reduces to a single 128-bit multiply, a right shift, and a small correction that handles negative dividends. With ideal compiler support the generated code consists of a `imul`/`mul` instruction followed by a `sar` and a conditional add, all of which fit in the processor’s integer pipeline.

Benchmarks on an Apple M4 Pro (ARM64) and a Snapdragon X1-26-100 showed a 10, 20 % higher throughput for the 86400 divisor compared with the built-in `/` operator. On x86 (AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D and Intel Core i7 MacBook Pro 2016) the new code was 5, 10 % faster for roughly 80 % of positive divisors and 60 % of negative divisors.

In the remaining cases throughput was slightly lower, but latency stayed competitive. The benchmark suite covered more than 40 divisors and reported per-divisor results for both throughput and latency.

## How to use the provided `fast_i64_floordiv_86400` function

The page supplies a ready-to-paste implementation for the common divisor 86400. The core of the function is the multiplier shown above; the rest of the code performs the multiply-shift and the sign-aware correction. The full snippet looks like this:

```cpp
inline int64_t fast_i64_floordiv_86400(int64_t x) {
    const int64_t M = ((__int128(1) << 79) / 86400 + 1);
    // implementation continues …
}
```

To integrate it:

1. Copy the function definition into a header or source file. The copyright notice at the top of the page permits verbatim copying under the MIT-style license.  
2. Replace occurrences of `x / 86400` with `fast_i64_floordiv_86400(x)`. The function returns the floor of the exact quotient, matching the mathematical definition.  
3. Compile with optimization flags that enable 128-bit arithmetic (`-march=native` on GCC/Clang, `/arch:AVX2` on MSVC). The compiler will usually inline the function and emit the multiply-shift sequence.  
4. Verify correctness with the provided boundary test that checks all values from `INT64_MIN` to `INT64_MAX` for the divisor 86400. The test file is part of the self-contained C++ generator linked from the article.

If a different constant divisor is needed, the same generator can produce a custom multiplier. The article includes a small C++ program that enumerates 65 535 divisors from -32768 to 32767 and emits a complete, self-contained implementation for each.

## The takeaway

Floor division is a small but frequent operation that most languages treat as a slow, built-in division. By using a 128-bit magic multiplier, the new algorithm replaces the division with a fast multiply-shift sequence that is correct for the full signed 64-bit range. On most modern CPUs this yields 5, 20 % higher throughput with comparable latency. Copy the `fast_i64_floordiv_86400` function, or generate a similar one for your own constant, to get the speed boost without sacrificing correctness.
